terms: Trapping of outgoing longwave radiation by atmospheric gases, warming the planet.
Principal anthropogenic greenhouse gas; concentration around 420 ppm in the 2020s, up from ~280 ppm pre-industrial.
Potent greenhouse gas with about 28× the warming power of CO₂ over 100 years.
Estimated total cumulative emissions consistent with a given warming target.
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established 1988, providing assessments of climate science.
Net change in energy balance of the climate system, measured in W/m².
UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, agreed at the Rio Earth Summit.
First binding emissions targets for developed countries; entered into force 2005.
Global climate accord aiming to limit warming to well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C.
Countries' self-set emissions plans submitted under Paris, updated every 5 years.
Five-yearly assessment of collective progress under the Paris Agreement.
Compensation mechanism for climate impacts beyond adaptation, agreed at COP27 in 2022.
Process amplifying initial change, e.g. ice-albedo feedback or methane from permafrost.
Process counteracting change, e.g. increased plant growth absorbing CO₂.
Actions to reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions.
Adjustments to limit harms or exploit benefits of actual or expected climate change.
Fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface; ice ~0.8, ocean ~0.06.
Technologies capturing CO₂ from emissions or air for storage underground.
Region receiving less than 250 mm precipitation per year, with high diurnal temperature range.
World's largest hot desert at approximately 9.2 million km², stretching across North Africa.
Dry channel that experiences flash floods during rare rainfall events.
Plant adapted to arid conditions through deep roots, small leaves or water storage.
Semi-arid transition zone south of the Sahara, particularly vulnerable to desertification.
African initiative since 2007 to plant trees across the Sahel to combat desertification.
Agreement designating Antarctica for peaceful, scientific use; in force from 1961.
Permanently frozen ground, ranging from continuous to sporadic, that thaws in surface 'active layer'.
Cold dense air flowing downhill from ice plateaux, often reaching destructive speeds.
Floating extension of glacier ice over the ocean.
Small crustacean that anchors the Antarctic food web supporting whales, seals and penguins.
Environmental protocol to the Antarctic Treaty designating the continent a 'natural reserve devoted to peace and science'.
Process of mountain building through tectonic collision, e.g. Himalayan orogeny from ~50 Ma.
Acute mountain sickness from low oxygen, beginning above ~2,500 m.
Net result of accumulation (snowfall) and ablation (melt and sublimation) over a glacier per year.
Glacial lake outburst flood, a major Himalayan hazard exacerbated by warming.
Term for the Himalayan-Tibetan region holding the largest ice mass outside the poles.
Tibetan ethnic group of north-eastern Nepal renowned for high-altitude expertise.
FAO definition: when all people have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food at all times.
Average daily kilocalories per person available for human consumption in a country.
Extreme food crisis classified as IPC Phase 5, with widespread starvation and excess mortality.
Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, headquartered in Rome.
Composite measure including undernourishment, child stunting, wasting and mortality.
Parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium spp., transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, killing over 600,000 people annually.
Bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted by airborne droplets, killing about 1.3 million people annually.
Epidemic spread over multiple countries or continents, e.g. COVID-19 declared by WHO 11 March 2020.
Living organism, often an arthropod, that transmits pathogens from one host to another.
Indirect protection from infection when a sufficient proportion of a population is immune.
Average number of secondary infections produced by one case in a fully susceptible population.
Insufficient intake of energy or essential nutrients, leading to stunting, wasting or micronutrient deficiencies.
Excess intake of calories, particularly from ultra-processed foods, leading to overweight and obesity.
Coexistence of undernutrition and overnutrition in the same population, household or individual.
Body Mass Index = mass(kg) / height(m)²; overweight ≥ 25, obese ≥ 30.
Low height-for-age caused by chronic undernutrition, especially in early childhood.
Shift from traditional diets toward energy-dense, processed foods as countries urbanise and incomes rise.
Lack of water resources to meet demand, common in arid regions.
Inadequate investment in water infrastructure despite sufficient resources.
Per capita water availability below 1,700 m³/year.
Large-scale transport of water from surplus to deficit regions, e.g. South-North Water Transfer Project (China).
Reducing water use through pricing, efficiency, leakage repair and awareness.
Removal of salt from seawater or brackish water to produce freshwater, energy-intensive but expanding in the Gulf and elsewhere.
Wearing away of channel bed and banks by hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and corrosion.
Movement of sediment by traction, saltation, suspension and solution.
Settling of sediment when river energy falls, forming features like floodplains and deltas.
Sinuous river bend formed by lateral erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank.
Built structures such as dams, levees and channel straightening for flood defence.
Non-structural approaches like floodplain zoning, afforestation and wetland restoration.
Closed system circulating water between atmosphere, land and oceans.
Area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, an open subsystem of the hydrological cycle.
Boundary separating one drainage basin from another.
Combined loss of water from soil (evaporation) and vegetation (transpiration).
Lateral movement of water through the soil layer towards streams.
Series of sea waves generated by underwater seismic, volcanic or landslide displacement.
26 December 2004 tsunami from a Mw 9.1-9.3 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake.
Maximum height a tsunami wave reaches inland above sea level.
Receding of the sea before a tsunami arrives — a critical natural warning.
Network established from 2006 to provide early tsunami warning in the Indian Ocean.
Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure ÷ Capacity, used to assess disaster risk.
Icelandic ice-capped stratovolcano whose 2010 eruption disrupted European aviation for several days.
Volcanic Explosivity Index, scaling eruptions from 0 (Hawaiian) to 8 (super-eruptions).
Fragmented material ejected from volcanoes including ash, lapilli and bombs.
Hot, high-speed mixture of gas, ash and rock fragments flowing downslope.
Volcanic mudflow especially associated with eruptions interacting with snow, ice or rain.
Volcanic centre fed by a fixed mantle plume, e.g. Hawaii.
Logarithmic measure of seismic energy release on the moment magnitude scale (Mw).
11 March 2011 magnitude 9.0 megathrust earthquake off northeast Japan.
12 January 2010 magnitude 7.0 earthquake near Port-au-Prince killing around 220,000 people.
Convergent boundary where one tectonic plate descends beneath another.
Process by which saturated soils behave like a liquid during shaking, damaging foundations.
Framework for analysing disasters by interaction of hazard and vulnerability.
Firm operating in multiple countries through foreign direct investment and global supply chains.
Geographically distributed system of value creation incorporating firms, suppliers and institutions.
Cross-border investment giving lasting control or influence over an enterprise.
Contracting out parts of production to independent suppliers.
Relocating production processes to another country, often within the same corporation.
Adaptation of global products to local tastes and regulations, e.g. McDonald's menu variation.
Spread of cultural elements (language, food, religion) from one society to another.
Mixing of cultural influences producing new forms, e.g. Tex-Mex cuisine, Afrobeats.
Dominance, often economic and cultural, of one group or country over others (Gramsci).
Joseph Nye's concept of influence through attraction rather than coercion.
UNDP composite of reproductive health, empowerment and labour participation.
Identity composed of multiple cultural references, often associated with migration and diaspora.
Process of intensifying economic, social, political and cultural integration across borders.
Composite index from KOF Swiss Economic Institute measuring economic, social and political dimensions.
Former index (2001-07) ranking countries on trade, capital flows, technology and political engagement.
Actual flows of goods, capital, people and information.
Legal and policy frameworks enabling cross-border flows.
Harvey's concept that transport and communication shrink the friction of distance.
Crutzen and Stoermer 2000 term for human-dominated epoch; AWG proposed 1950s Great Acceleration as start; IUGS rejected formal designation 2024.
Atmosphere, high seas, outer space and Antarctica; managed via UNFCCC, UNCLOS, Outer Space Treaty 1967 and Antarctic Treaty.
KOF Index measures economic, social and political dimensions; AT Kearney index; global trade-to-GDP rose from 25% in 1970 to 60% in 2008.
Roland Robertson 1995 term; global processes adapted locally; McDonald's Maharaja Mac in India a textbook example.
Submarine fibre-optic cables carry 99% of internet traffic; 552 active cables totalling 1.4 million km as of 2023.
Rockstrom et al 2009 framework; nine boundaries including biosphere integrity and biogeochemical flows; six transgressed by 2023 update.

geographic-themes-three-from-the-sl-list.d: Geographic Themes (Three from the SL list)
terms: The maximum number of visitors a destination can support without unacceptable environmental damage or a declining visitor experience; key in the tourism theme.
The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries; an open system with inputs, stores, flows and outputs, central to the freshwater theme.
Cold high-altitude and hot arid regions with low population density, where harsh conditions and fragile ecosystems limit human activity.
In the geophysical hazards theme, risk is the chance of harm, depending on the hazard event, people's exposure, their vulnerability and capacity to cope.
IB DP Geography HL students study three optional themes chosen from a list including freshwater, oceans, extreme environments, geophysical hazards, tourism, food and health, and urban environments.
The rising share of a population living in towns and cities; the urban environments theme examines its causes, megacities and management responses.

hl-core-extension-global-interactions-po.d: HL Core Extension: Global Interactions (Power, Places & Networks; Human Development & Diversity; Global Risks & Resilience)
terms: Indian diaspora 32 million worldwide 2022; remittances totalled $111 billion in 2022 (top global recipient).
UNCTAD World Investment Report; global FDI peaked at $2.0 trillion in 2007 before financial crisis; recovered post-pandemic.
Saskia Sassen's Global City 1991 identified New York, London, Tokyo as command points; GaWC ranks Alpha+ cities.
Composite Index of National Capability (CINC) Singer 1972; includes population, urban, iron-steel, energy, military expenditure.
Joseph Nye 1990 concept of co-optive power through culture, values and policies; Brand Finance Global Soft Power Index ranks states annually.
Immanuel Wallerstein 1974 divides world economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery; capitalist division of labour since 16th century.
Alonso's 1964 model: land value decreases with distance from CBD; can be tested with rateable values fieldwork.
Compares observed vs expected frequencies in categorical data; suitable for testing distribution patterns.
Consent for questionnaires, anonymisation, environmental impact of sampling, BPS Code; risk assessment before fieldwork.
Testable prediction (e.g. 'pebble size decreases downstream'); needs null version for statistical testing.
Non-parametric correlation test for ranked data; rs from minus 1 to plus 1; tested at 0.05 significance level.
Measure of spread around mean; 68% of normal distribution within 1 SD; used to compare variability.
El Niño-Southern Oscillation: coupled ocean-atmosphere mode of variability in the tropical Pacific.
Warm phase of ENSO with weakened trade winds and warmer eastern Pacific.
Cool phase of ENSO with strengthened trade winds and cooler eastern Pacific.
Global ocean conveyor belt driven by temperature and salinity gradients.
Vertical movement of cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface supporting major fisheries.
Linkage of weather patterns across great distances, e.g. ENSO effects on Indian monsoon.
Loss of symbiotic zooxanthellae from coral polyps under thermal stress, leaving skeletons white.
Reduction in ocean pH (around 8.2 to 8.1 since 1750) as oceans absorb CO₂.
Increase in ocean volume as water warms, contributing about half of recent sea-level rise.
Worldwide sea-level change due to variation in water volume.
Local sea-level change due to vertical land movement.
Salt-tolerant coastal forests acting as nurseries, sediment traps and storm buffers.
Low, long waves with stronger swash than backwash, building beaches.
High, short waves with stronger backwash than swash, eroding beaches.
Movement of sediment along a coast in a zig-zag pattern under oblique waves.
Coastal compartment in which inputs, transfers and outputs of sediment can be considered as a closed system.
Depositional landform extending out from the coast where it changes direction.
Bar of sand or shingle connecting an island to the mainland.
Five-stage model describing the shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as countries develop.
Number of live births per 1,000 population per year.
Number of deaths per 1,000 population per year.
Difference between CBR and CDR, expressed as a percentage.
Average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime; replacement level ~2.1.
Post-industrial stage in which birth rates fall below death rates and populations decline.
Negative conditions encouraging people to leave an origin: conflict, poverty, environmental degradation.
Positive conditions attracting people to a destination: jobs, schools, safety.
Movement of people within a country, especially rural-urban migration.
Movement of people across national borders, voluntary or forced.
Money sent home by migrants, a major source of foreign exchange for many LICs.
Increase in the proportion of population living in urban areas, now over 55% globally.
Bar chart showing the proportion of males and females in age cohorts.
Pyramid with a broad base, common in LICs and many MICs with high fertility.
Pyramid with a narrow base and wide upper sections, typical of post-industrial HICs.
Ratio of dependents (under 15 and over 65) to working-age population (15-64).
Economic boost arising when working-age population is large relative to dependents.
Group of individuals born during the same period and ageing together through the pyramid.
Disputes between states over territory, resources, identity or influence.
Overlapping claims by China, Vietnam, Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan over reefs and waters.
Chinese cartographic claim covering most of the South China Sea, rejected by 2016 PCA ruling.
Intergovernmental forum of 8 Arctic states established 1996 to coordinate cooperation.
Long-running unresolved dispute with no active large-scale fighting, e.g. Nagorno-Karabakh prior to 2020.
Economic and political measures imposed on states to coerce policy change.
Standardisation of shipping containers (TEU) from the 1950s, transforming global logistics.
Fibre-optic cables crossing oceans, carrying over 95% of intercontinental data traffic.
Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, messaging network central to global payments.
Network model with central hubs connecting peripheral nodes, common in aviation.
Strategic geographic constraint on movement, e.g. Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal.
Chinese strategy launched 2013 financing infrastructure across Eurasia, Africa and Latin America.
State exerting comprehensive global influence across military, economic, technological and cultural domains.
Dominant state setting norms and structures within an international system.
Group of major emerging economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, expanded 2024).
Group of seven major advanced economies meeting annually.
Forum of 19 countries plus the European Union covering most of world GDP.
Halford Mackinder's 1904 thesis that control of the Eurasian 'heartland' confers global power.

geographic-perspectives-global-change-po.d: Geographic Perspectives: Global Change (Population Distribution, Global Climate, Global Resource Consumption)
terms: The total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by a person, product or country, usually expressed as CO2 equivalent.
The degree to which a place or group can be harmed by climate change, shaped by exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity.
The area of productive land and water needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its waste, compared with Earth's biocapacity.
An urban area with more than 10 million inhabitants; most new megacities are growing in Asia and Africa.
Global population is spread very unevenly; climate, relief and economic opportunity concentrate people in coastal lowlands and cities.
Reliable access to affordable food, water and energy; the water-food-energy nexus shows how stress on one resource affects the others.

geographic-themes-freshwater-oceans-coas.d: Geographic Themes: Freshwater / Oceans & Coastal Margins / Extreme Environments / Geophysical Hazards / Leisure, Tourism & Sport / Food & Health / Urban Environments
terms: Hard engineering (groynes, sea walls), soft engineering (beach nourishment, dune planting), and managed realignment.
Thermal stress expels symbiotic zooxanthellae; Great Barrier Reef saw mass bleaching in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020 and 2022.
Quasi-periodic Pacific climate pattern alternating El Nino, La Nina and neutral phases; affects global weather every 2-7 years.
IPCC AR6 2021 projects 0.28-1.01 m rise by 2100 under SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5 scenarios.
Global ocean conveyor driven by temperature and salinity differences; AMOC weakened 15% since mid-20th century.
UN Convention on the Law of the Sea defined 12-nautical-mile territorial waters and 200-nm Exclusive Economic Zones.
Urban agglomeration with more than 10 million inhabitants.
Urban region exceeding 20 million inhabitants, e.g. Tokyo, Delhi.
Ordering of settlements by population and function.
City disproportionately larger than the next in a national urban system, e.g. Bangkok.
City exerting global influence through finance, culture and politics, e.g. New York, London, Tokyo.
Movement of population from cities to smaller settlements and rural areas, observed in some HICs.
Sustainable development is 'meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' (1987).
Beddington Zero Energy Development in south London, completed 2002, a low-energy eco-village of 100 homes.
Bus Rapid Transit, a high-capacity bus system using dedicated lanes pioneered in Curitiba in 1974.
Planning model favouring high density, mixed use and walkability to reduce energy and travel.
Urban model using ICT and data to optimise services and infrastructure.
Network of natural and semi-natural features delivering ecosystem services in cities.
UN-Habitat definition: settlement lacking durable housing, sufficient space, water, sanitation or security of tenure.
Housing built outside legal frameworks, often on land the residents do not own.
Mumbai neighbourhood of around 1 million people across roughly 2.1 km², blending residential and industrial use.
Urban policies in which residents upgrade their own homes with state-supplied materials or services.
Approach providing serviced plots for residents to build upon themselves.
Legal right to occupy and use land, central to investment in housing improvements.
